content.title: About
content.content: Roast pork is a cut of pork cooked in the oven at moderate heat until a golden crust forms. The meat is tender, juicy, and carries a distinctive aroma that is enhanced by herbs and spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide.
Roasting retains most nutrients, including protein, iron, and B‑vitamins.
Traditional marinades often feature soy sauce, honey, garlic, and rosemary.
The crust on roast pork contains aromatic compounds that add flavor and texture.
In many cuisines roast pork is served with apple sauce or sauerkraut.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Pork provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of zinc and iron
items.content: These minerals are important for immune health, DNA synthesis, and oxygen transport.

items.title: Contains selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports thyroid function.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: The protein and creatine in pork help maintain muscle strength during active training.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Some pork cuts can be fatty; choose lean cuts and watch portion sizes.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked pork may contain pathogens (e.g., Salmonella); cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to pork proteins.

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: Very salty marinades can increase sodium intake, which is undesirable for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot roast pork sliced thinly. It pairs well with mashed potatoes, roasted vegetables, apple‑based sauces, or mustard. Leftovers can be stored in the fridge and used in salads, sandwiches, or soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the roast to room temperature, then place it in an airtight container. Store in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it keeps quality for 2–3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 71 °C before serving.

shrimp-and-noodles-with-cream-or-white-s.title: Shrimp and noodles with cream or white sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish combines broad noodles, sautéed shrimp, and a smooth cream or white sauce made from cream, milk and seasonings. Shrimp cook quickly, while the sauce gives the meal a velvety texture and notes of garlic, lemon and fresh herbs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp are one of the most consumed seafood items worldwide, with demand growing over 5 % annually.
Durum‑wheat noodles retain their shape even after prolonged simmering in sauce.
Cream sauce is often thickened with a roux of flour and butter before adding 10‑20 % cream.
The recipe can be adapted for lighter diets by using low‑fat milk or plant‑based cream alternatives.
Asian variations often add ginger and soy sauce for a more pronounced flavor.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Shrimp provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: 100 g of shrimp contain roughly 99 kcal, making them suitable for weight‑control meals.

items.title: Source of omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA in shrimp contribute to heart and brain health.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for blood formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace elements support immune defense and antioxidant processes.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Sodium in the sauce
items.content: Prepared sauces can be salty; adjust added salt to taste.

items.title: Foodborne pathogens
items.content: Improperly stored shrimp may harbor bacteria that cause food poisoning.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the noodles al dente, sauté the shrimp with garlic, then add cream, milk, lemon juice and seasonings. Toss the sauce with the noodles, garnish with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan or a lemon wedge, and serve hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw shrimp refrigerated at 0‑2 °C for up to 2 days or freeze them. Leftover cooked dish should be consumed within 24 hours, stored in an airtight container in the fridge.

content.title: About
content.content: Vodka and diet cola (5420) is a popular mixed drink that combines the neutral flavor of vodka with the zero‑calorie sweetness of diet cola. It is often served over ice in tall glasses and used as a light alcoholic beverage for parties.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The vodka‑diet cola combo originated in the United States in the 1970s as an alternative to sweeter cocktails.
Diet cola contains artificial sweeteners such as aspartame or sucralose, making the drink virtually calorie‑free.
Standard vodka is usually 40 % ABV, but in the mix its concentration drops to 5‑10 % depending on the ratio.
The drink is often called a “tall” because it is served in tall glasses.
In some countries it is recommended to sip the drink slowly to avoid a rapid rise in blood alcohol level.

items.title: Moderate consumption may promote relaxation
items.content: Small amounts of alcohol have a calming effect, reducing stress and creating a sense of well‑being.

items.title: Low‑calorie cocktail option
items.content: Diet cola contributes virtually no calories, so this mix is less energy‑dense than traditional sweet cocktails.

items.title: Hydration from ice
items.content: Serving the drink over ice adds water, which can partially offset the dehydrating effect of alcohol.

items.title: Alcohol intoxication
items.content: Vodka contains ethanol, which in excess leads to impaired coordination, slower reaction times, and risk of alcohol poisoning.

items.title: Artificial sweetener sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals react to aspartame or sucralose with headaches or allergic‑type symptoms.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Alcohol can amplify the effects of sedatives and certain anti‑inflammatory drugs.

items.title: Increased stomach acidity
items.content: Cola’s acidic components may worsen reflux or cause discomfort in people with gastritis.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Pour 30‑50 ml of vodka into a tall glass, add ice, and top up with diet cola. Optionally garnish with a lemon or lime wedge.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store vodka in a cool, dark place with the bottle tightly sealed. Keep opened diet cola refrigerated to maintain carbonation.
